title: Enhancing Persona Following at Decoding Time via Dynamic Importance Estimation for Role-Playing Agents
one_liner: Estimate which parts of a character profile matter in the current scene, then bias word choice toward those parts during generation.
lead: A role-playing agent is given a character profile and must answer in ways that fit that character. A fixed prompt often fails because not every trait matters equally in every situation. This paper argues that persona following should change with context. Its method, Persona Dynamic Decoding, first scores how important each persona attribute is for the current scene, then uses those scores to steer decoding so that highly relevant traits influence the next words more strongly. The core claim is that context-dependent persona weighting improves consistency because the agent emphasizes the right parts of the profile at the right time instead of treating every trait as equally active all the time.

problem.h2: Why static persona control breaks in changing scenes
paras: A character profile can include many facts, goals, and behavior tendencies. In one conversation turn, only some of those details actually matter. A fixed prompt usually places the full profile in front of the model, but it does not say which parts should dominate now.

This creates two common errors. The agent may ignore an important trait because the scene changed and the prompt does not update which traits should matter most. Or it may overuse an irrelevant trait and sound forced. The hard part is not storing the persona. The hard part is deciding which persona details should carry the most weight in the current context.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Score persona traits by current relevance, then use those scores to tilt decoding toward responses that match the most relevant traits.

steps.text: The system receives the persona attributes together with the current conversation state.
A scoring module assigns each persona attribute a context-dependent importance value.
The high-importance traits contribute more to the reward used during generation.
The generation scores are adjusted so that candidate continuations that better match the active traits become more likely.
The answer reflects the persona details that matter most in this scene because the decoding process gave them more influence.

paras: The paper changes persona control from a static prompt feature into a turn-by-turn decision process. The main object is no longer the full profile alone. It is the profile together with a scene-specific importance score for each attribute.
object.object: persona attributes weighted by current scene importance

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: active persona pressure
hidden.name: how strongly each profile trait should influence the current reply
paras: The key quantity is not whether a trait exists in the profile. It is how much that trait should matter for the next response. For example, a character's job may matter in one exchange, while a social habit matters in another.

The method tries to estimate this shifting pressure directly. When the estimate is accurate, the decoder can emphasize the right persona signals and suppress the less relevant ones. That helps because the response is then guided by the traits that actually explain the current behavior.

heat.caption: The goal is to place the strongest pressure on the persona details that the current scene actually activates.

reads.html: A trait should matter only when the current scene gives that trait a real reason to matter.
The system estimates scene-conditioned trait importance and uses those scores during decoding so that persona alignment reflects current context instead of a fixed profile average.

mechanism.h2: Why dynamic weighting can beat a static prompt
paras: A static prompt treats the profile as one block of text. That keeps all traits present, but it does not decide which ones should dominate each turn. Dynamic weighting adds that missing decision. It says which profile elements deserve more control right now.

This can help because language generation involves many close alternatives. If the decoding rule nudges the model toward words and phrases that fit the currently important persona traits, small local choices accumulate into a more consistent reply. The gain comes from using context to allocate influence instead of spreading influence evenly across the full profile.

stages.s: score trait importance for this turn
weight persona rewards by those scores

math.h2: A compact statement of the decoding rule
math.words: Score each candidate continuation by combining the model's base score with a weighted sum of persona-match rewards, where each weight comes from the current scene.
symbols: the model's ordinary score for a candidate continuation before persona steering
the estimated current importance of persona trait i
how well the candidate continuation matches persona trait i
add the weighted contribution from all persona traits
the score used to choose the next continuation

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a character is both careful and humorous.
In a scene about safety, the system gives careful importance 0.8 and humorous importance 0.2.
Candidate A is a cautious reply with base_score(candidate) = 5, persona_reward_careful(candidate) = 3, and persona_reward_humorous(candidate) = 0.
Candidate B is a joke with base_score(candidate) = 5, persona_reward_careful(candidate) = 0, and persona_reward_humorous(candidate) = 3.
Candidate A wins because the active trait for this scene is careful behavior.

math.note: The method matters when the importance values change with context, because that is what lets the same profile produce different but still in-character behavior across scenes.

charts.title: Static persona prompting
charts.note: A fixed prompt can preserve some role detail, but it reacts weakly to scene changes because every trait is always presented in the same way.

charts.title: Dynamic persona decoding
charts.note: The method improves role following by changing which traits get the most influence on each turn.

items.html: If the system misreads the scene, it can amplify the wrong trait, so the reply may still follow the profile but in the wrong way for that moment.
Conflicting or vague persona attributes make weighting harder, because the system has no clear basis for deciding which trait should dominate.
If the reward term overrides the model's base fluency too much, the answer can become stiff or repetitive because the decoder is forcing persona alignment at the expense of natural phrasing.
The approach works when the system estimates current trait importance accurately and uses those scores gently enough that the reply stays natural while remaining in character.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a small role-playing benchmark with a few character profiles and several scene types for each character. For every turn, show the profile, the current scene, the importance score assigned to each trait, and the final reply. Compare static prompting against dynamic weighting on two checks: does the reply reflect the relevant trait for the current scene, and does it stay natural. The demo should let a reader watch trait weights move from one turn to the next so that the reason for each reply is visible.
demo.metric_eq: role_fit = scene_relevant_trait_matches / total_checked_traits; drift_rate = out_of_character_replies / total_replies
demo.closing: The key result is not just that the reply mentions the persona. It is that the right part of the persona shows up for the current scene.
